paras: The lynching of Lucian Langdon and William Harrison took place at Prineville, Wasco county, Oregon, early on Friday, March 17, 1882, when masked men overpowered a deputy sheriff's guard, shot Langdon and hanged Harrison from a bridge. Langdon had been arrested on the charge of killing two neighbors in a land dispute, while papers reported that nothing connected Harrison, his employee, to the killings. The wire account ran nationally, sometimes under headlines calling Harrison innocent.

A letter from Prineville dated March 15 reported that A. H. Crooks and his son-in-law S. J. Jorry had been shot dead on Willow Creek, behind Langdon's house. A passer-by, Garret Maupis, heard the shots, found the two men dead and saw Langdon riding away with a Winchester rifle. According to an informant interviewed by an Oregonian reporter, Langdon had fenced a strip of disputed land between the ranches, and when Crooks and Jorry began cutting a tree on it, a quarrel ended with Langdon firing both barrels of a shotgun. The Corvallis Gazette, calling the dead man Aron Crooks, son of 'the Hon. Crooks of Linn county,' said the two were killed 'while peacebly and quietly at work.'

A posse of Prineville citizens arrested Langdon and his hired man Harrison at Langdon's residence and turned them over to Deputy Sheriff Lucky, who placed a guard of four men over them. Langdon and his wife both asked the arresting party to protect him from mob violence, and the party promised to do so. The Oregonian's informant told it differently: Langdon, headed off riding away from his house, surrendered, saying he feared lynching and had meant to give himself up.

About half-past two on Friday morning, at the Jackson House in Prineville, a masked mob of twelve or fifteen covered each member of the guard with a pistol and opened fire on Langdon, who was killed almost instantly. The men then dragged Harrison to the Ochoco bridge and hanged him to the trestle work. In the informant's version, Harrison was sleeping in the hotel, came down to the street after the shooting, and was caught by a riata tied to a saddle and dragged to Crooked river bridge, dead before he got there.

A coroner's inquest was held over both bodies, but none of the lynchers had been identified; Langdon left a wife and two young children. The deputy sheriff said a blanket had been thrown over his head, and the Oregonian's informant reported that many believed the posse had helped the lynchers, while an Oregonian correspondent censured the Sheriff for not resisting. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The fullest wire, datelined The Dalles, ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under the headline 'Horrible Work of a Mob' and called the killings a 'terrible outrage.' Its closing line, that Harrison's 'only offense' was his employment by Langdon, shaped eastern headlines such as the Richmond Dispatch's 'Lynching an Innocent Man.' Condensed versions ran on March 21 in the New-York Tribune ('Lynch Law in Oregon'), the Savannah Morning News and the Wheeling Register, and later in weekly digests from Maryland to Pennsylvania. Many garbled the names, calling Langdon 'Tucson' or 'Tuscan Langler', and placed the lynching at Dallas, Oregon, or Dallas, Texas.

In regional comment, the Oregonian's informant called Harrison's hanging 'a deliberate murder' and described the lynchers as cowboys new to southern Wasco county, 'prototypes of their brethren in Arizona and Texas.' Under 'The Prineville Horror,' the Washington Standard in Olympia hoped for 'no ill-timed mercy' for the perpetrators, while the Vancouver Independent judged Langdon 'undoubtedly guilty' even as it saw no proof against Harrison. None of the papers mentioned the race of anyone involved.

Accounts differ on the guard (four men in the Dalles wire, eight per the informant), on whether it was overpowered or stood aside, and on whether Harrison was a prisoner or a hotel guest seized in the street. They also differ on timing: the wire gives 2:30 Friday morning, the Washington Standard the night of the 17th, and the informant's sequence puts the arrest on Friday morning with the lynching that night.

Two men were killed by a masked party of twelve to fifteen (A2, A4) or 'a dozen' (A16, A17) who took them from a deputy sheriff's guard, Langdon being held on the charge of killing Crooks and Jory (A6, A2); no paper reports the race of either victim.

The Dalles wire (A2, A4) and the Oregonian reporter's separate interview with a man from Prineville (A3) agree that a mob overpowered the guard, shot Langdon and hanged Harrison, as do regional papers (A16, A17, A18).

accounts.label: Dalles wire
accounts.gist: A Prineville posse arrested Langdon and Harrison at Langdon's home and turned them over to Deputy Sheriff Lucky; at the Jackson House a masked mob of twelve or fifteen covered the guard of four, shot Langdon and hanged Harrison at the Ochoco bridge; an inquest was held.

accounts.label: Oregonian reporter's informant from Prineville
accounts.gist: Langdon surrendered while riding toward Prineville, was held under a guard of eight that offered no resistance, and many believed the posse helped; Harrison, not a prisoner but sleeping at the hotel, was roped by a riata and dragged behind a horse to Crooked river bridge.

accounts.label: Washington Territory papers
accounts.gist: A dozen or more masked men overpowered the Sheriff's posse, shot Langdon and hanged Harrison to a stringer of the bridge; one paper judged Langdon 'undoubtedly guilty'.

framing.detail: The Dalles wire called it a 'terrible outrage' under the Sacramento headline 'Horrible Work of a Mob' and said Harrison's only offense was his employment.
Eastern papers ran condensed wire under 'Lynch Law in Oregon', 'An Oregon Lynching', 'A Double Lynching', 'Lynching an Innocent Man' and 'Lynched by an Armed Band', often misplacing it at Dallas.
The Oregonian informant called Harrison's hanging 'a deliberate murder' and likened the cowboy lynchers to those of Arizona and Texas.
The Washington Standard's 'The Prineville Horror' called for the law to close on the 'perpetrators of the inhuman act'.
The Vancouver Independent saw no proof against Harrison but called Langdon 'undoubtedly guilty' and expected 'a heated discussion on mob law'.

conflicts.note: Regional and first wire reports give Lucian/Lucien; 'Tucson' appears in condensed eastern wires and is likely a garble.
